title: The JVM: compilation, bytecode, execution and LTS releases

videos.script: Every lesson in this course asks you to type something. So the first thing this lesson does is give you somewhere to type it. {{lab}} One Ubuntu machine, your own or a virtual one, and two packages from Ubuntu's archive: a Java Development Kit, version 25, and Maven. One line to type, and about three hundred megabytes to download. {{installed}} Then a look at what arrived. Thirty programs, and one surprise: a second Java you did not ask for. {{fails}} Three ways the setup goes wrong, each produced on purpose, each with a message that names its own cause. {{bytecode}} Then the first program. Java does not turn it into machine code. It turns it into bytecode, for a machine that does not exist, and a program called java pretends to be that machine. {{releases}} Last, versions. A new Java arrives every six months, and every two years one of them is kept alive for a long time. Twenty-five is that one. By the end you have a working JDK, and you know what it does to a file before anything runs.
